overview.text: A wave is a traveling disturbance that carries energy from one place to another; in many waves, the material involved oscillates around its usual position rather than traveling along with the disturbance. Waves include sound, ripples on water, earthquakes, and light. Mechanical waves, such as sound, need a substance called a medium to travel through, while electromagnetic waves, including light, can cross empty space. Waves are distinguished by how their disturbance moves: in a transverse wave it is perpendicular to the direction the wave travels, and in a longitudinal wave it is parallel. Some waves combine both kinds of motion.

key_facts.text: Waves transfer energy, but mechanical waves generally do not carry the medium’s material along with them; its particles oscillate around equilibrium.
Sound and water waves are mechanical waves that require a medium; electromagnetic waves such as light do not.
Transverse disturbances move perpendicular to wave travel; longitudinal disturbances move parallel to it. Sound in air is longitudinal.
Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium; wavelength is the distance between matching points, such as consecutive crests.
Frequency counts cycles passing a point per unit time; it is the inverse of period and is commonly measured in hertz (Hz).
